awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Effective, Affordable, UV Treatment Technology for Microbiologically Contaminated Water
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader/commercial impact of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is in the development of a novel inexpensive, adaptable point-of-use water treatment device. It deploys commonly used ultraviolet (UV) light disinfection technology in a simple pitcher-shaped, countertop, household appliance. It operates using electricity when available but can also be powered by a rechargeable battery. Anyone can safely operate it to produce all the drinking water needed after a city’s water treatment or distribution systems are damaged by a flood or earthquake or other natural disaster. Thus, the product can have significant value in addressing the U.S. incident and emergency management challenges. Microbiologically contaminated drinking water contributes to more than 500,000 deaths annually. Globally, about a billion people boil their water every day to make sure it is safe. The proposed product can meet their needs more safely while meaningfully reducing carbon emissions. This project is also in alignment with the 2022 U.S. Global Water Strategy that calls for increased water security where it is needed most.
 

This SBIR Phase I project will focus on the design of an instrumented UV appliance. This will be aided by light transmission modeling in non-cylindrical vessels to assure uniform and adequate exposure of water to the UV light and appropriately locating UV-C LED lamps and UV transmittance monitors to achieve those goals. The device will be experimentally tested with controlled microbial challenges with the goal of demonstrating that the appliance conforms to World Health Organization’s standards for household water treatment technologies for a broad array of contaminated water sources. It is thought that discrete UV intensity monitoring can be correlated with UV-C dose so that performance can be adjusted for water with varying levels of microbial contamination. The appliance will also incorporate sensor capabilities to automatically log, and report use data to support the potential compilation of carbon credits.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Project Outcomes Report for SBIR Phase 1 NSF Grant

 

Effective, Affordable, UV Treatment Technology for

Microbiologically Contaminated Water

 

NSF Award 2449174

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Submitted by DayZero Water LLC

July 2026

 

 

 

Introduction

DayZero Water LLC, through an SBIR National Science Foundation Phase 1 grant, made progress toward launching a new household water treatment product for use across the world. 

 

The current reality is that people in developing world cities must provide treatment of the water that comes from their faucets to ensure it is safe to drink. 

 

DayZero Water’s product specifically targets this need. It provides a safer, more convenient treatment method than boiling, which is the predominately-used method. The product uses a proven drinking water treatment method, ultraviolet (UV) disinfection, but packages it in a simple, affordable product, one that is suitable even for families without running water to their homes or for those with an intermittent power supply.

Intellectual Merit (advances in knowledge)

Through the NSF grant, DayZero Water investigated the use of LEDs to produce the UV output needed for drinking water treatment. LEDs are being used for this purpose but not to the extent of the traditional mercury vapor lamps. The industry is moving toward greater use of LEDs for this purpose but at this time, they are less energy-efficient than mercury lamps.

 

We examined how to optimize the use of multiple LEDs in a way that provides the best level of treatment. Traditional flow-through UV products shine the UV light along a length of pipe with the dose controlled by both the output of the UV lamps and the flow rate of water through the system. This concept has to be modified for a batch container. Our NSF work included examining the position of UV LEDs inside or around the perimeter of various container shapes. We also investigated methods to implement mixing to make sure that all water passes in close proximity to the UV LEDs during the treatment cycle.

 

A related aspect of our work was to develop and refine a mathematical model of the UV treatment process in a batch container. A model can provide significant value for designing a product because it allows the design to be optimized to a great extent before advancing to physical testing to confirm success.

 

We investigated was the incorporation of a sensor to confirm that the water can be treated by UV disinfection. The technical challenges to using a sensor included sensor selection and its location within a container. Sensors providing the highest response to the UVC wavelength are expensive. Less-sensitive, broad-wavelength sensors are much less expensive, but it was necessary to determine if they could provide a high enough response to meet the need, especially when the shape of the container limits their proximity to the LEDs.

We selected two brands and models of LEDs for our research work, with varying costs and outputs. Based on the number of LEDs and their power draw, we then determined the rechargeable battery type, sizing, and cost. We found that a battery system capable of operating ten treatment cycles, treating sufficient water for a family for two days of electricity interruption, could be affordably incorporated into the product.

 

One other technical area of research was in tracking the volume of water treated. Because our product is a substitute for boiling, with certification it can generate carbon credits. A common weakness of carbon credits is verification. We investigated a methodology for tracking product use and reporting these authenticated data to a central receiving station. It was determined that low-energy Bluetooth communication to the owner’s phone and then periodic communication from the owner’s phone via the Internet would provide the most robust system.

Broader Impacts

Widespread adoption of an inexpensive, reliable UV household water treatment product will lead to measurable public health and climate change benefits.

 

Currently, boiling is the most commonly used household water treatment approach. But families often cannot boil enough to meet their immediate needs and resort to drinking unsafe supplies when their boiled water runs out. This contributes to stubbornly high waterborne disease morbidity and mortality rates. Additionally, many people, especially children, suffer burns every year from cookstoves and boiling water. Our UV product would directly address these public health needs.

 

Since boiling is often performed over cookstoves using biofuels, the replacement of boiling with UV disinfection is a significant means of reducing carbon emissions. Considering that 1.5 billion people rely on boiling each day to make their water safe and that about half of these people boil their water over charcoal- or wood-fueled cookstoves, the carbon emission reductions will make a positive difference for our planet.
